one_liner: Python code generator emitting per-weight-matrix x86 assembly SpMM kernels for pruned networks; beats LIBXSMM sparse and dense BLAS above ~70% sparsity.
what_it_does: Given a fixed, unstructured-sparse FP32 weight matrix A and the column count of the dense activation matrix B, it generates an assembly kernel computing A*B (optionally with bias/ReLU epilogue) specialized to that exact sparsity pattern, assembles it with gcc into a .so, and calls it. The Python API is a SpMM class (constructor takes the dense array with zeros, then compile() and run()); the C++ path goes through driver_cpu.cpp and the autotune_cpu_random.sh script. There is also a block-sparse INT8 generator. It is a kernel generator, not a drop-in BLAS or inference engine.
how_it_is_fast: The generator unrolls the whole sparse matrix into straight-line code: each nonzero is a vbroadcastss of the weight followed by vfmadd231ps against a row slice of B whose offset is baked into the instruction as an immediate, so there is no index decoding at run time. It adapts dense-GEMM register blocking (AT x CT microkernel tiles) plus split-K tiling over the reduction dimension, and stores values in a custom order matching the kernel's traversal. Tile sizes are autotuned per matrix by brute-force search over AT/CT/B_blocks.
when_to_use: CPU inference of models pruned to 80-95% unstructured sparsity with weights fixed at deploy time (pruneBERT-style fully connected / 1x1 conv layers).
x86-64 servers with AVX2 or AVX-512 where you can afford an offline code-generation and autotune step per weight matrix.
Research or benchmarking of sparse FP32 SpMM kernels against LIBXSMM/MKL, since it exposes kernel-level timing.
Single-threaded or low-core-count deployments, where its advantage over LIBXSMM is largest (2.5x geomean on Intel single-thread vs 1.7x at 4 threads).
when_not_to_use: Sparsity below about 70%: the paper puts the break-even with dense BLAS there, so dense MKL/oneDNN wins.
Dynamic or activation sparsity: patterns must be known at code-generation time; the paper says it does not handle ReLU-induced activation sparsity.

Production end-to-end inference: the sparse-convolution generator and the inference engine from the paper were never open-sourced; the README itself points end-to-end users to Neural Magic DeepSparse.
Multi-threaded throughput on AMD (breakeven with LIBXSMM at 4 threads) or aarch64 (code paths for ARM exist in the generator but no ARM results are published).
Anything needing maintenance or support: last commit 2022, single author who says he works on it sparingly.

integration.dependencies: Python + NumPy for the generator; gcc to assemble the generated .s; C++ driver needs cnpy and the autotune script calls icc with -mkl and OpenMP
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 for driver_cpu.cpp (per autotune script); otherwise not documented
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2 (AVX-512 used when present); Linux assumed (reads /proc/cpuinfo)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the driver parallelizes by splitting work across OpenMP threads with start/end ranges

gotchas: Each generated kernel is valid only for one weight sparsity pattern and one dense column count (C_dim); new weights or batch shapes require regeneration.
fastsparse.py has module-level test code that loads matrix.npy and benchmarks on import, and compile() writes out.s/out.cpp to the current directory and shells out via os.system.
The Python API adds noticeable ctypes overhead on small matrices; the paper's numbers come from the C++ driver.
autotune_cpu_random.sh passes -D CT=$1 (the A dimension) to the driver instead of $CT, so the tuning script's driver build looks buggy; check before trusting its output.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over LIBXSMM when weights are highly sparse (90%+) and fixed, since LIBXSMM is the faster general choice for dense small GEMM and its sparse path lost 2.5x here single-threaded; for LLM inference with quantized rather than pruned weights, T-MAC or llamafile tinyBLAS fit better.
verified_claims_summary: The author's own arXiv paper (2101.07948) measured generated FP32 SpMM kernels on an AWS Intel Xeon Platinum 8124M (AVX-512) and AMD Epyc 7R32 (AVX2): 2.5x geomean over LIBXSMM single-threaded on Intel (1.3x on AMD), 1.7x on Intel and breakeven on AMD at 4 threads, about 4x over dense MKL/OpenBLAS at 95% sparsity, sparse conv 3.0x/4.8x (Intel) and 3.4x/6.3x (AMD) over dense oneDNN at 90/95% sparsity, and up to 5x pruneBERT throughput over OpenVINO; compiler and flags for the baselines are not given in the paper.
status_note: Abandoned since September 2022 but Apache-2.0 and only a handful of Python files, so the generator can be vendored; the parts needed for end-to-end inference were never released.
